title: Given a count N followed by N numbers read one by one, draw a flowchart to find and print the largest among them. Start, read N, read the first number into max, initialize i = 2, loop while i <= N doing read x and if x > max then max = x and i = i + 1, print max, End. Input: 5 then 3 9 2 15 7, Expected Output: 15.
shortTitle: Largest of N Numbers — read N numbers one by one and print the largest

s1_definition.profdef: Finding the maximum of a stream of N values is a single-pass scan that keeps a running maximum. You seed the running maximum with the first value, then read each remaining value and replace the running maximum whenever a larger value appears. This is an online algorithm with constant extra memory and linear time, because it never needs to store all the values at once.
s1_definition.analogy: National Bank of India processes a day's transactions one at a time and wants the single largest transaction amount for a suspicious-activity report, without holding the whole day in memory. It remembers the biggest seen so far, starts with the first transaction, and updates the record whenever a bigger one arrives. For amounts three, nine, two, fifteen, seven the largest is fifteen.
s1_definition.oneliner: Find the maximum of N values in one pass by seeding with the first value and replacing the running maximum whenever a larger value arrives.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Finding the maximum of a stream of N values is a single-pass scan that keeps a running maximum. You seed the running maximum with the first value, then read each remaining value and replace the running maximum whenever a larger value appears. This is an online algorithm with constant extra memory and linear time, because it never needs to store all the values at once.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** National Bank of India processes a day's transactions one at a time and wants the single largest transaction amount for a suspicious-activity report, without holding the whole day in memory. It remembers the biggest seen so far, starts with the first transaction, and updates the record whenever a bigger one arrives. For amounts three, nine, two, fifteen, seven the largest is fifteen.

**One line to remember:** Find the maximum of N values in one pass by seeding with the first value and replacing the running maximum whenever a larger value arrives.

sections.s2_technical:
The algorithm reads the count N, then reads the first value directly into the running maximum called max. This seeding with a real value is important because it avoids the trap of initializing max to zero, which would be wrong if all values were negative. From the second value onward, the loop reads each value x, and if x is greater than max it updates max to x. After all N values, max holds the largest.

The comparison for money uses BigDecimal's compareTo, so `x.compareTo(max) > 0` means x is strictly greater. I use strict greater-than so the first occurrence of the maximum is kept on ties, though for finding a maximum it does not change the resulting value. The loop runs from the second value to the Nth, which is N minus one comparisons, and uses only the single max variable, so the space is constant regardless of how many values stream through.

A senior nuance is robustness: I validate that N is at least one, because the maximum of zero values is undefined, and I handle streaming input so the algorithm works even when the values arrive from a file or a message queue rather than being held in a list. If the values were already in a collection, I could use the stream max method with a comparator, but the explicit single-pass scan is the right mental model and is exactly what you need when the data does not fit in memory. Throughout, keeping amounts as BigDecimal ensures the comparison is exact.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India needs the largest transaction amount of the day for a suspicious-activity report, reading transactions one at a time. We must track the running maximum across a stream. This is exactly the seed-then-scan algorithm.

Problem 2 — Transactions can include negative adjustments, so seeding max at zero would be wrong. This is exactly why we seed max with the first actual value read.

Problem 3 — The day's transactions should not all be held in memory at once. This is exactly why the single-pass scan with one max variable is used.

Our mini-project builds a `MaxFinder` with a `largest(List<BigDecimal> amounts)` method that scans in one pass, and a `LargestOfNDemo` runnable that finds fifteen as the largest of three, nine, two, fifteen, seven.

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: N = 5, values 3, 9, 2, 15, 7.

Step 1 — The first value, three, is read directly into max, so max starts as a real value rather than zero. This protects against all-negative inputs.

Step 2 — The second value nine is compared to max three. Nine is greater, so max becomes nine.

Step 3 — The third value two is compared to max nine. Two is not greater, so max stays nine.

Step 4 — The fourth value fifteen is compared to max nine. Fifteen is greater, so max becomes fifteen. The fifth value seven is compared to fifteen and is not greater, so max stays fifteen.

Step 5 — After all five values, max holds fifteen, which is returned and logged as the largest transaction of the day. Only one variable was kept throughout, so memory stayed constant.

Final output:

```
2026-11-01 00:02:00 [INFO] Largest transaction of the day = Rs.15
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: N=5, stream: 3, 9, 2, 15, 7
    │
    ▼
  max = first = 3
    │
    ▼
  scan rest:
    x=9  → 9>3   → max=9
    x=2  → 2>9   → max=9
    x=15 → 15>9  → max=15
    x=7  → 7>15  → max=15
    │
    ▼
  Output: 15
```
sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Single-Pass Maximum ═══

  ┌─ Principles ─────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: finder only computes the maximum          │
  │  Seed max with FIRST value (not 0) → negatives safe│
  │  O(N) time, O(1) extra space → streaming-friendly│
  │  compareTo → exact money comparison            │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌──────────────────────────────┐
  │           MaxFinder          │
  │ ──────────────────────────── │
  │ + largest(List<BigDecimal>)  │ throws IllegalArgumentException
  │     : BigDecimal             │
  └──────────────────────────────┘

  Contract for largest(amounts):
    Pre:  amounts non-null, non-empty
    Post: returns the numerically greatest element
    Throws: IllegalArgumentException if empty/null

  Call Chain:
  1. largest([3,9,2,15,7])
  2.   max = 3
  3.   compare rest → max=9 → 9 → 15 → 15
  4.   return 15
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the largest of N values read one by one is a single-pass scan that keeps a running maximum. You seed the running maximum with the first value, then read each remaining value and replace the running maximum whenever a larger value appears, and after the last value the running maximum is the answer. For the values three, nine, two, fifteen, seven the running maximum climbs to nine then to fifteen and stays there, so the result is fifteen.

The detail I always call out is the seeding. You must seed the running maximum with the first actual value, not with zero, because if every value were negative, a zero seed would wrongly report zero as the maximum. Seeding with a real value also makes the algorithm correct for any range. The scan itself is linear time with constant extra memory, because it keeps only the single maximum variable and never needs to hold all the values at once, which is exactly what you want when the data streams in from a file or a queue and may not fit in memory. For money I compare with BigDecimal's compareTo so the comparison is exact.

In my banking work at National Bank of India, I used this for a suspicious-activity report that needed the single largest transaction of the day without loading the whole day into memory. I wrote a MaxFinder whose largest method seeds the maximum with the first amount and scans the rest in one pass, comparing with compareTo and validating that there is at least one value. For a day of three, nine, two, fifteen, and seven it reported fifteen. The lesson I stress is that a maximum scan is trivial to write but has a real correctness trap in the seed, and seeding with the first element rather than zero is what makes it correct for every possible input.
